topic: Conditional Branching in Assembly and its Relation to High-Level Control Flow
explanation: High-level programming languages like C use control flow statements (if, else, while, etc.) to alter the execution sequence.  Compilers translate these into assembly instructions, primarily using conditional and unconditional branches. Understanding this translation is crucial for optimizing performance and debugging low-level code.  Conditional branches allow the processor to selectively execute different code paths based on the result of a condition, impacting performance by controlling instruction-level parallelism and pipeline behavior.  The number of branches in assembly may differ from the number of conditional statements in the source code due to compiler optimizations.

code_example:
; C: if (A == B) { True; } else { False; }

; Comparison sets RFLAGS register
CMP RAX, RBX        ; A vs B
JNE L_ELSE_42       ; Jump if Not Equal

; --- True Block (Executed if A=B)
MOV RCX, 1          ; True Result
JMP L_END_42        ; Skip False block

L_ELSE_42:
; --- False Block (Executed if A!=B)
MOV RCX, 0          ; False Result

L_END_42:
; Execution continues (Merge Point)
